# Products and bands

Every product is a GeoTIFF, described in Python by a small metadata record. The
record holds the product's identity, such as burst, date and type, and
`FileManager.get_product_path()` turns it into the file's location. This page
describes what the files contain.

## Bands and units

Each product type has a fixed set of bands, named in the GeoTIFF's band
descriptions:

| Product | Bands | Values |
|---|---|---|
| RTC backscatter | `gamma0`, `scattering_area` | Linear power; area without units |
| GTC backscatter | `beta0` | Linear power |
| Coherence | `coherence` | 0 to 1, without units |
| Interferogram | `ifg_real`, `ifg_imag`, `intensity_primary`, `intensity_secondary` | Uncalibrated |
| Composite | Same quantity as its inputs | As the inputs, or decibels with `decibel=True` |
| `QA-NUM` | `num_obs` | Number of contributing acquisitions |
| `QA-CQM` | `cqm` | Composite quality, linear or decibels |

Backscatter is stored as linear power, not decibels. Convert with
`10 * log10(value)` only after averaging, since the mean of decibels is not the
decibel of the mean. The `scattering_area` band describes how much ground each
pixel covers; [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains
how composites use it.

The interferogram's phase is the angle of the complex number
`ifg_real + i·ifg_imag`, in radians from −π to π. Its two intensity bands show
the brightness of each acquisition.

## Missing values

Pixels without data are `NaN`, for example outside the burst. Keep them
missing in statistics and plots rather than replacing them with zero. The one
exception is `QA-NUM`, an integer layer that marks pixels without data as 0. Rasterio
returns them masked with `src.read(1, masked=True)`.

## Metadata tags

Each GeoTIFF also carries tags that say how to read it and how it was made.
They include the units of the stored values, the acquisition dates, the DEM,
and the SNAP and s1bursts versions:

```{.python}
import rasterio

with rasterio.open(fm.get_product_path(product)) as src:
    print(src.descriptions)
    print(src.tags())
```

These tags make a file understandable on its own, even when separated from the
code that wrote it. Their names follow the vocabulary of the
[CEOS-ARD SAR specification](https://ceos.org/ard/), so a term can be looked up
there. s1bursts borrows the vocabulary only and does not claim conformance with
the specification.

## Filenames

Filenames contain only what is needed to tell products apart, such as product
type, orbit, footprint, polarization and date. Processing settings are not part
of the name, which is why a product made with different settings is skipped
rather than reprocessed. Record your settings alongside your results.
